blocks.md: This lesson covers the book's section on **Capacity for Trajectories**. Read the excerpt, then test yourself below.

blocks.source: Vol III, Agent Economics, § Capacity for Trajectories
blocks.md: Admitting one 20-minute repair trajectory per minute holds 20 sandboxes open concurrently while sending 60 model calls per minute to the inference pool. Sizing an agent platform therefore differs from sizing a stateless web service. Work enters the platform as a multi-step trajectory, but the operations that saturate hardware consist of individual model calls, tool executions, and resource leases, each with its own arrival rate, holding interval, and concurrency limit.

blocks.title: What the section covers
blocks.md:
In the book this section runs through:

- Residence, service, and quota
- The price of queueing
- Dedicated capacity vs. per-token APIs

blocks.prompt: Think first: In two or three sentences, explain why Trajectory goodput matters for the system this section describes.
blocks.md: Compare your answer with the book's claim: Accepted tasks per unit time is the platform's deliverable, so sustaining goodput G at acceptance alpha requires admitting G/alpha trajectories and any change that lowers acceptance raises offered load.

questions.q: The section **Capacity for Trajectories** develops one of the chapter's claims. Which one?
options: Speculative decoding pays only when the accepted-draft rate shortens the output-bound critical path by more than draft and verification work add to the bill.
A speedup g applied to a fraction f of the measured critical path gives T' = T[(1-f) + f/g] and a ceiling of 1/(1-f), which a baseline profile reveals before anything is bought.
Near saturation queueing wait grows like rho/(1-rho), so a modest throughput gain from higher utilization costs a multiple in wait that compounds across every serial step of a trajectory.

Accepted tasks per unit time is the platform's deliverable, so sustaining goodput G at acceptance alpha requires admitting G/alpha trajectories and any change that lowers acceptance raises offered load.
